findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the calling thread until the HTTP call completes or the 5s timeout fires. In an asyncio server this blocks the entire event loop, so every other in-flight request on that worker stalls for the duration — the opposite of what the `async` keyword suggests to callers who `await` it.

Use the existing httpx async path instead, mirroring `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7: accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with`) and `await client.get(...)`. If a synchronous client is genuinely required, run it via `asyncio.to_thread`/`run_in_executor` rather than calling it directly on the loop, and drop the now-unneeded `requests` import on line 2.

A test that runs this coroutine concurrently with another task and asserts the other task isn't delayed would catch this class of bug.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is f-string-interpolated into the path of an internal, presumably unauthenticated-by-network-position service (`https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`) with no validation or percent-encoding. If `tenant_id` reaches this function from request data (path/query/body/JSON), a value such as `../../admin/keys` or `1?force=true` or `1/../../tenants` lets the caller reach other paths and query parameters on the internal billing host and have the JSON body returned to them — a server-side request forgery against an internal endpoint. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a redirect from the billing host would be followed silently.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[0-9]+$`) before use, or `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`, and consider `allow_redirects=False`. The same interpolation exists in `fetch_plan` on line 6, so the guard is best applied at the call sites or in a shared helper.

findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` are caught and discarded here — Ctrl-C or a worker shutdown signal raised while inside `_client.send` will be silently converted into a normal `return None` instead of propagating. Narrow this to `except Exception:` (and, if the client has a typed transport error, prefer that). The PR description says "catch and log", but no logging call was added, so every push failure — network error, auth failure, serialization bug — now disappears with no trace at all. Add a `logger.warning(..., exc_info=True)` before returning.

findings.title: Rate limit bypass: try_consume checks and updates outside _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control to the event loop with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) does acquire.

Two consequences, both attacker-reachable by simply issuing requests concurrently (the normal capability of any network client):

1. Check-then-act bypass: N coroutines can all read the same `current`, all find `current + cost <= LIMIT`, and all return `True`, admitting up to N times the intended cost.
2. Lost update: because each writer stores its own `current + cost` rather than incrementing, concurrent calls overwrite each other. The counter permanently undercounts, so the bypass is not a one-off overshoot — a client that keeps requests in flight can keep the stored counter arbitrarily far below its real consumption and never be limited at all.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the existing lock and removing the yield point between read and write:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

Note the entry point that calls `try_consume` is not present in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot name the concrete handler; the exploit requires only that some request path reaches it concurrently, which is the premise of a per-tenant limiter.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter without holding _lock

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed insert
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error`, which is always nil, and return it. The result is that `WriteSettlement` reports success for every call that reaches the insert, whether or not the settlement row was actually written — a caller in the end-of-day batch has no way to distinguish a persisted settlement from a dropped one, and nothing will retry or reconcile it.

If the intent really is "log and continue", make that explicit at the call site rather than in the writer: return the error from `db.Exec` and let the batch loop decide to log and proceed. Otherwise, at minimum, return the captured error:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

Note also the contrast with `WriteEntry` directly above (line 7-8), which propagates its `Exec` error — callers reasonably assume the same contract here.

Callers inspecting the return value to decide what to re-send will re-send recipients that already succeeded in a later batch, or mis-report the failure count.

findings.title: compute_rounding silently changes half-cent boundary (>= 0.5 -> > 0.5)
findings.body:
This PR is described as a rename-only change, but `compute_rounding` also changes its comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For the exact boundary input `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — i.e. exact half-cent remainders round down instead of up. In a billing package this is a money-affecting behaviour change: totals for any line with a 0.5 remainder shift by one cent, and it will not be caught by anyone reviewing this as a mechanical rename.

If the change is unintended, restore `>=`. If it is intended (e.g. switching to round-half-down), it should be split into its own commit with a test covering `remainder_cents == 0.5` and a note about the effect on existing invoices.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge()`, but `billing/gateway.py` states plainly that `charge` is NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge. A transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, connection reset, 5xx on the response path) will be retried and will create a second — and possibly third — charge against the customer's card. The retry on `fetch_charge` is fine because `get_charge` is a safe GET; this one is not equivalent.

The gateway docstring names the fix: pass an `Idempotency-Key` header, generated once per logical charge attempt and reused across retries, so the gateway collapses duplicates. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards such a key, this wrapper should not retry — or should retry only on errors that provably occurred before the request was sent.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can double-charge (no Idempotency-Key)

Without an Idempotency-Key header (which the underlying `charge` function documents as required for safe retries), this function could silently create duplicate charges on retry. The function must either: (1) document that callers must pass an Idempotency-Key, (2) implement it internally, or (3) not retry this call. At minimum, document the idempotency requirement and constraint.

findings.title: Content-Length drives buffer pre-allocation (declared-length memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` on an S3 UploadPart request comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header (or the equivalent field the S3 frontend parses out of it). Previously the pool-backed RW grew only as bytes actually arrived from `body`, so peak memory tracked the real payload. After this change the full declared size is reserved up front, before `io.Copy` has read a single byte, so a client can claim `Content-Length: 5368709120` and send one byte — or nothing — and still force the server to reserve gigabytes. Repeat across concurrent connections and the process OOMs; the attacker pays almost no bandwidth.

Suggested fixes: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` using the S3 5 GiB part cap or a configured limit), skip the reservation entirely when `contentLength` is negative or zero (chunked/unknown bodies typically report `-1`, and it is unclear from this diff whether `Reserve` tolerates a negative argument), and enforce that the bytes actually read (`n`) match the declared length before accepting the part.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from untrusted Content-Length before any body is read

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unknown/absent Content-Length (-1) passed to Reserve unguarded

If Reserve panics, over-allocates, or silently misbehaves on such inputs, nothing in the test suite would catch it — the change would ship with a false sense of safety, which is especially concerning since this PR's stated purpose is related to a declared-length allocation CVE.

findings.title: Default scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext on an explicit `False`; every other value — including the common case where `is_secure` is absent and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value) as a request for plaintext, so callers that never set `is_secure` now have their S3 request URL built as `http://...`, sending the AWS-signed request over an unencrypted channel. Restore the opt-out semantics, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"` if the ternary form is preferred.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ S3 scheme default changed from HTTPS to HTTP

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP after ternary inversion
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was fail-secure: TLS was used unless a caller explicitly opted out with `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is fail-open: `request.meta.get("is_secure")` returns `None` whenever the key is not set — which is the normal case for any request that did not deliberately configure it — so `scheme` becomes `"http"` and the URL built on line 6 is fetched over an unencrypted connection.

Consequences: the AWS request signature / `Authorization` header and any session token travel in cleartext, and the response body (private bucket contents) is exposed. A network-position attacker can read credentials and replay the signed request, or tamper with the returned object, which is then parsed by the spider.

Fix: restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or if the simpler ternary is wanted, default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: Default scheme behavior change is untested
findings.body: The old code defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new code defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This flips the default for requests where is_secure is unset (None/missing), which affects whether S3 requests are sent over plaintext HTTP by default. No test file is present in this diff to verify scheme selection for the unset/None case, the True case, and the False case.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
`request.Method` (fully attacker-controlled, it is the verb on the inbound HTTP request) flows into `action`, which becomes the `ResourceAction` used for the access-control decision. The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to `"delete"`; the new two-branch form maps everything that is not GET/HEAD — including DELETE — to `"push"`.

Per pkg/api/config/config.go the three actions are deliberately distinct: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." After this change any principal holding only `push` on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and pass authorization, destroying existing tags/blobs. Equivalently, the `delete` grant becomes unreachable and meaningless.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` before the push assignment) so the delete permission is still consulted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorizes as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: Documented ActionDelete is now unreachable
findings.body: The code previously mapped http.MethodDelete to an 'delete' action, as documented in pkg/api/config/config.go. This diff collapses all non-GET/HEAD methods to 'push', making the documented ActionDelete contract impossible to reach. Callers relying on the documented three-action system will not get the 'delete' action they expect for DELETE requests. Either restore the DELETE mapping or update the documented contract in config/config.go to reflect that only two actions ('pull' and 'push') now exist.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-push mapping change
findings.body: The change collapses distinct 'delete' action handling into 'push', meaning an account with push-but-not-delete permission would now be authorized to delete resources via HTTP DELETE. This contradicts the repository's documented access model (config.go comments explicitly say push and delete are distinct so an account can push without deleting). No test in this diff exercises this mapping, so a regression here (or reverting to correct behavior) would go undetected.

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods flips from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` to any method not explicitly enumerated (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, and anything else). The new inverted condition sends all of those to `"push"`, so requests that previously only needed read access — most notably CORS preflight `OPTIONS` — will now be rejected for pull-only clients. If the stricter default is intended it should be stated explicitly; otherwise enumerate the write methods (POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE) rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, discarding the just-written entry
findings.body: After storing `tenant` at line 10, the guard on line 11 checks the cache size and, when exceeded, calls `_CACHE.clear()` — which removes every entry, including the one this call just inserted. Two consequences: (1) the write-through this function exists to perform is silently undone on the call that crosses the threshold, so a following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the value was just fetched; (2) every other tenant is evicted at once, so the next burst of `get_tenant` calls all miss and fall through to whatever refetches them. If the intent is a bounded cache, evict a single entry (or use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics) and do it *before* inserting the new value, so the fresh entry survives.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id can force a full flush of the shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` writes `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` for whatever key it is handed (line 10) and, once the shared dict exceeds 1000 entries, discards *every* entry with `_CACHE.clear()` (lines 11\u201312). If `tenant_id` is reachable from request data, a caller can insert ~1000 junk keys and repeatedly evict all legitimately cached tenants, turning every subsequent `get_tenant` into a miss and pushing that load onto `_fetch`'s backing store. The cost to the attacker is one cheap request per insert; the cost to the system is a cold cache for all tenants.

Two mitigations, either of which removes the lever: (a) reject/authorise `tenant_id` before it is used as a cache key \u2014 only cache keys the caller is entitled to and that `_fetch` resolved to a real tenant (currently a `None`/error result from `_fetch` is cached just as happily as a real one); and (b) replace the all-or-nothing `clear()` with bounded per-key eviction (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an LRU/TTL map), so that crossing the size limit evicts one entry rather than the whole working set.

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh function has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behaviour: fetching fresh data, writing it into the shared _CACHE, and clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the eviction threshold, the clear-vs-evict-one strategy, or the write-through to _CACHE were broken (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, or clearing on every call), nothing would fail.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body: Line 7 of README.md documents the flag as `--workers`, but the code on line 6 of cli.py now names it `--concurrency`. A user following the README will pass the wrong flag name and the tool will reject it. Update the documentation to match the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename silently changes argparse dest from workers to concurrency
findings.body:
`p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` produced a namespace attribute `args.workers`; the renamed `--concurrency` produces `args.concurrency`. Every site that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime (argparse namespaces have no default for the removed name), and any script or CI job invoking `--workers` will fail with `unrecognized arguments`. The PR description says the intent is to match the *internal* flag name, which suggests internal readers exist.

If the internal name is already `concurrency`, confirm every reader was updated; otherwise keep the old surface working, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)` so existing invocations keep parsing, and grep for `\.workers` before merging.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring says the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but line 4 now returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. Any caller relying on the documented contract (expecting an integer) will break. Update the docstring to describe the new return format: e.g., 'Return a dictionary mapping day to count of API calls for that day.'

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without changing the contract
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. The function name and signature are unchanged, so every existing caller that does arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (e.g. `if monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the code signals the change. Either return both (`total` plus `by_day`), add a new function / keyword flag for the breakdown, or update every caller and the docstring in this change.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, a breaking API contract change. Nothing in this diff exercises the new return shape or verifies callers/consumers still work with it. Add a test asserting the returned mapping structure (e.g., {day: count}) for a known set of rows, and check for regressions in any caller expecting an int.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter as `page_size`
findings.body:
The docstring on line 6 describes `page_size` as a parameter, but the function signature on line 1 has renamed this parameter to `limit`. Callers reading the docstring will look for a `page_size` parameter that no longer exists, causing confusion and potential errors. Update the docstring to reference `limit` instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking module-level function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller that passes it by keyword (`list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)`) will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime; positional callers are unaffected, so this failure will only surface for some call sites. No callers were retrieved for this review, so the blast radius is unverified — please grep for `page_size=` across the repo, and if external consumers exist, either keep `page_size` as a deprecated alias (`def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)`) or bump the API version.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped on new request() path — TLS checks may not apply
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` before calling `prep = req.prepare()` and `self.send(prep)`. Nothing carries `verify` or `cert` forward, and `send()` (lines 365-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no verification arguments either.

Consequence: a caller that explicitly pins a CA bundle (`verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem'`) or supplies a client certificate (`cert=(...)`) gets neither — the call succeeds while the intended trust anchor / client auth is not in effect. If the adapter's implicit default is not `verify=True`, this silently disables server-certificate validation entirely and exposes every HTTPS request on this path to an active network attacker (MITM). The same omission applies to `timeout` (line 141), leaving requests able to hang indefinitely against a slow/hostile peer.

Thread `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` through to `adapter.send()` (or onto the prepared request), and make the adapter's verification default explicit rather than inherited.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch and session defaults
findings.body:
The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor — a caller doing `session.get(url, timeout=1, verify=False)` now gets an unbounded, certificate-verifying request with no error. `return_response=False` previously returned the request object rather than a response; it now always returns the response.

Equally, the old path merged session state (`self.headers`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.cookies`, `self.config`, `self.hooks`) into the per-call values; the new path assigns the raw arguments only, so `Session(headers=...)` / `session.auth = ...` have no effect. Silently ignoring a parameter is worse than raising: either wire these through to `prepare()`/`send()` or drop them from the signature until they are.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send kills pooling; close() no longer releases anything
findings.body:
`send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call. Assuming the adapter owns a `PoolManager` (which is what the removed `init_poolmanager` did on the Session), this means a brand-new connection pool per request: no connection reuse at all, and the pools/sockets are only reclaimed whenever GC gets to them. At the same time `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so `with Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` no longer release any connections — the docstring's contract ("closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections") is gone with nothing replacing it.

Hold the adapter on the Session (e.g. build it in `__init__` or a mount map) and have `close()` clear it.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module uses the explicit relative form (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import: it only resolves under Python 2 without `absolute_import`, and raises `ImportError: No module named adapters` on Python 3 or anywhere `requests/` is not itself on `sys.path`. Since it is a module-level import, the failure takes down the whole `requests.sessions` module, not just `send()`. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Session refactor (close/request/send) has no accompanying tests
findings.body: This diff removes PoolManager ownership, makes close() a no-op (line 132), rewrites request() to build and send a PreparedRequest (lines 134-167), and changes send() to delegate to a new HTTPAdapter (lines 363-367). None of these behaviour changes are exercised by any test in this diff. If close() silently stops releasing connections, or if the new request()/send() path drops a parameter (e.g. timeout, verify, cert, config, return_response, which are accepted but never used), nothing would fail — the code would just run and do the wrong thing.

findings.title: Stale docstring removed but behavior changed
findings.body: The `close()` method had a docstring explaining it disposes of internal state by closing the PoolManager. That docstring was deleted when the method body changed to `pass`, making the documentation removal look correct. However, the docstring described the *old* behavior (closing pooled connections), and the new behavior (doing nothing) is now undocumented. A caller reading the code or help text would not know that `close()` is now a no-op.

findings.title: Public method `send()` loses its docstring
findings.body: The `send()` method is a public API (called by `request()` and potentially by external callers). The old one-liner docstring "Send a given PreparedRequest." is retained on line 364, but the implementation changes significantly—it now instantiates an HTTPAdapter and delegates to it. The docstring does not explain what the adapter does or whether this method is the recommended way to send requests. For a public method, the contract is unclear.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
The old implementation guaranteed that `cookies` always returned a `Cookie.SimpleCookie` — on a malformed header it called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which iterated the (partially loaded) SimpleCookie and left `_cookies` as a dict-like object. The new version sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it, so callers get `None` instead of a mapping.

Concrete breakage with an attacker- or client-supplied malformed `Cookie:` header:
- `web.py:321` `if name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning every `get_cookie()` call into a 500.
- `web.py:367` `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError` on `None`.
- The cached `None` also short-circuits the `hasattr` guard, so the failure is sticky for the whole request.

Fix: keep the invariant by resetting to an empty cookie jar, e.g. `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the `except` branch (the request object can't clear response cookies, so the old `clear_all_cookies()` side effect can't be preserved here — if that behaviour matters, re-add it on the RequestHandler side).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: No test coverage for cookie parsing/error-handling behavior change
findings.body: The cookies property was moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (leaving self._cookies as an empty SimpleCookie), while now a parse failure sets self._cookies = None. This changes the contract for callers like get_cookie and clear_all_cookies, which now call self.request.cookies.iterkeys()/__getitem__ on a value that could be None, causing an AttributeError instead of silently doing nothing. Nothing in the diff exercises the malformed-Cookie-header path or verifies get_cookie/clear_all_cookies behavior after the move, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Missing .strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the leading space that virtually every client sends: `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----X"` produces the element `" boundary=----X"`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop completes without breaking, the `for ... else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", and the body is never parsed. Every multipart POST (file uploads and form fields) silently loses its arguments and files — a functional regression versus the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` test, which was whitespace-insensitive. Fix by partitioning the stripped field: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Content-Type parameters not stripped; ' boundary=' never matches

findings.title: No test covers the rewritten multipart boundary parsing
findings.body: The change to scan all Content-Type parameters for 'boundary' (rather than assuming it's the trailing field) is a meaningful behavior change to multipart parsing, but no test file is included in this diff. As written, the split on ';' does not strip whitespace, so a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' yields k=' boundary' (with a leading space) which never equals 'boundary', meaning the new code would silently fail to find the boundary in the common case where fields are separated by '; ' rather than ';'. A test exercising a realistic Content-Type header with a space after the semicolon would have caught this.

findings.title: Boundary value is not unquoted and parameter name match is case-sensitive
findings.body: RFC 2046 permits (and some clients emit) a quoted boundary, e.g. `boundary="--ABC"`; `v` will then include the quotes and `_parse_mime_body` will not match the delimiter in the body, so the parts are lost. Likewise parameter names are case-insensitive in HTTP, so `Boundary=` is skipped. Both were already true before this change, but since this hunk is the new central place where the parameter is parsed, consider `k.lower() == "boundary"` and stripping a surrounding pair of double quotes from `v`.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing ignores '?' and '#', enabling host-check bypass
findings.body:
`get_host` splits the authority off using only `://`, `/`, `@` and `:`. It never terminates the authority at a query (`?`) or fragment (`#`) delimiter, so for `http://trusted.example?@attacker.example` or `http://trusted.example#@attacker.example` the `'@' in url` branch on line 94 strips everything up to the `@` and returns `attacker.example` as the host. `urllib.parse`/`urlparse` returns `trusted.example` for both of these, because the authority ends at the first `?` or `#`.

The sink is whatever connection code consumes the `(scheme, host, port)` tuple: any caller that validates a user-supplied URL against an allowlist with a stdlib parser and then hands the same string to urllib3 will connect to a different host than it approved (classic SSRF / allowlist bypass). Consider deferring to `urlsplit`, or at minimum truncating `url` at the first `?` or `#` before the `@` and `:` handling. Relatedly, line 95 splits on the *first* `@` while RFC 3986 userinfo ends at the *last* `@`, which is a second source of parser disagreement.

This is a lift-and-shift of existing behaviour rather than newly written logic, but the diff is the place where this parser becomes the single shared entry point for all callers, so it is worth fixing here.

findings.title: New parsing/formatting logic added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: make_headers and get_host contain multiple branches (accept_encoding as str/list/other, basic_auth encoding, url parsing with scheme/path/auth/port splitting, and the malformed-port error path) that are being lifted into a new shared module for reuse by other callers, but no test file is present in the diff. If get_host's port-parsing logic broke (e.g. wrong split order, off-by-one in slicing 'proto://', or the error message's stray %s), or make_headers mis-joined accept_encoding lists, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message contains an unsubstituted %s
findings.body: The exception message is built with a `%s` placeholder but no formatting operand, so a caller parsing `google.com:http` sees the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL failed. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (and note `url` has already been truncated to the host part by lines 91-97, so you may want to capture the original argument before mutating it).

findings.title: Unicode/tuple accept_encoding is silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The type dispatch only recognises `str` and `list`. On Python 2 a `unicode` value such as `u'identity'` — and on either version a tuple such as `('gzip',)` — falls into the `else` branch and is silently overwritten with `'gzip,deflate'`, which is the opposite of what the caller asked for. Since the module already depends on `six`, use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` and accept any non-string iterable for the join branch.

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns a list, True, or None depending on path
findings.body: The docstring promises a boolean, but the select branch returns the readable-socket list from `select(...)[0]`, the poll branch returns `True`, and the poll branch falling through the loop returns `None`. Callers using truthiness are fine, but any caller doing an identity/equality comparison against `True`/`False` will behave differently per platform. Wrap the select result in `bool(...)` and add an explicit `return False` after the loop.

findings.title: No test exercises rejection of an invalid `direction` value
findings.body: The new validation raises ValueError when either `sort` or `direction` is not an allowlisted key, and `direction` is interpolated directly into the SQL string (line 17) just like `sort` is. The only added negative test (`test_rejects_an_unknown_sort_key`) only passes a bad `sort` value with the default `direction`; no test ever passes an invalid `direction` (e.g. `direction="; DROP TABLE invoices --"`). If the `direction not in DIRECTIONS` check were ever removed, weakened, or subtly broken (e.g. changed to only check `sort`), nothing in this suite would fail.

findings.title: Click output format changed despite "types only" description
findings.body: The old click branch returned `click at ${x}`; the new one returns `click at ${x}, ${y}`. This is an observable change to the function's return value, not a type-only refactor, so any caller, log parser or snapshot test asserting on the click string will now mismatch. Either restore the single-coordinate format or make the format change explicit in the PR description and update the affected assertions. Note also that `event.y` is only valid if the `click` variant of the union actually declares `y` — the previous code reached it through an assertion cast (`event as { x: number; y: number }`), which would have compiled even if the declared variant only had `x`.

findings.title: No test verifies describe() output for click/key events
findings.body: The switch statement now handles formatting for both event kinds, replacing unsafe casts with type narrowing. If the format strings were wrong (e.g. wrong property order, missing space, or a case falling through), nothing in this diff would catch it since no test file is included and none was retrieved from the repo.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now returns a URL, not the constructed string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location = location` stored exactly the value the caller passed (normally a `str`). After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `URL` object has no `startswith` method, so such callers will raise `AttributeError`, and `url_obj == "…"` comparisons will silently evaluate to `False`. Additionally `URL()` normalises its input (percent-encoding, default-port stripping, etc.), so even `str(exc.location)` may not round-trip to the original string.

If the goal is just to avoid constructing the `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local: `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`. If exposing a `URL` is intentional, it is a breaking public API change that needs a docs update and a deprecation path (e.g. a separate `location_url` property).

Note the `Location` header itself is unaffected — both versions emit `str(URL(location))`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `.location` type change can silently break redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: location attribute now stores URL object, not string as documented
findings.body: The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'the string it was constructed with', but this change now stores a `URL` object instead. Code that relies on this contract—such as comparisons with `str.startswith()` mentioned in the docs—will break. Either update the documentation to reflect that it now stores a URL object, or preserve the original string value.

findings.title: No test guards location's documented str type/behavior
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned a `URL` instance instead of the original string, changing its type. The docs (web_reference.rst) explicitly say `location` is 'the string it was constructed with' and that application code calls `str.startswith` on it — a `URL` object does not support that. Nothing in this diff includes a test asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or exercising `.startswith` on it, so this regression would ship silently.

findings.title: readany can return b"" before EOF after dropping the wait loop
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that its future is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, and explicitly requires callers to re-check their condition after waking. With `while` replaced by `if`, a single spurious/chunk-boundary wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `_eof` still false, so `readany()` returns `b""` even though the stream is not finished. Callers treat an empty return from `readany()` as EOF, so this silently truncates bodies. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-checked after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ while→if lets readany return a false EOF on a spurious wakeup

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed behavior: re-check no longer required
findings.body: The `_wait()` docstring at lines 1-8 documents that 'a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived.' This docstring was written to justify why `_wait()` needs to be called in a loop. However, the diff changes line 5 from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof:` to `if not self._buffer and not self._eof:`, meaning the caller no longer re-checks the condition—it only waits once. If this behavioral change is intentional, the docstring must be updated to reflect that one wake is now sufficient and no re-check is necessary. If the docstring describes the correct behavior, then the `while` loop should be restored.

findings.title: No test exercises spurious-wake re-check for readany()
findings.body: The change from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to `if not self._buffer and not self._eof` removes the re-check after waking, relying on the docstring's claim that a single wake is always followed by data or eof. If a spurious wake occurs (the referenced docstring for _wait explicitly warns callers must re-check their condition after waking, implying this can happen), readany() would now return an empty/incorrect result instead of continuing to wait. No test in this diff exercises a wake with no data still in buffer and not eof to confirm readany() behaves correctly, so a regression here would not be caught.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328): inside the `requests` package this line is interpreted as an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist, so importing `requests.sessions` — and therefore `requests` itself — raises `ImportError`/`ModuleNotFoundError`. Even on Python 2, where it resolves to `requests/adapters.py`, it now silently defers to any top-level `adapters` module that happens to be installed or sitting on `sys.path`, giving a wrong `HTTPAdapter`. This is not the "same module, cleaner form": restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or use the fully-qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`).

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows sys.path shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path` instead: under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) it will only find a *top-level* module named `adapters`, and `sys.path[0]` is the invoking script's directory (or the empty string / cwd for `-c`, `-m` and interactive use). Any `adapters.py` an attacker can place in one of those directories — a shared working directory, a world-writable deployment dir, an unpacked archive the app `chdir`s into — is imported in place of the library's own module, and whatever it exports as `HTTPAdapter` becomes the object every `Session` uses to mount HTTP/HTTPS transports. That object controls TLS verification, proxies and where requests are actually sent, so shadowing it yields silent MITM or exfiltration of every request the process makes, with code execution at import time as a bonus.

Independently of the hijack, this is very likely a plain breakage: on Python 3 there is no implicit relative import, so `import requests` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` unless the package directory happens to be on `sys.path`.

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Removing None guard breaks get_cookie on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is not always a mapping. The `cookies` property in `tornado/httpserver.py` documents and implements an explicit `None` return: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that," with `if self._cookies is None: return None`. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed Cookie header — turning a benign client-supplied header into a 500. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`) or, if the intent is really to make the attribute total, change the producer in `httpserver.py` to return an empty mapping instead of `None` and update its docstring — but that is a separate, wider change affecting every consumer.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard: malformed Cookie header causes TypeError/500

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The change removes the `is not None` guard on `self.request.cookies` based on the claim that cookies is always a mapping. But the repository's own httpserver.py docstring states cookies is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. If that is still true, `name in self.request.cookies` will raise TypeError instead of returning default. No test exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for normal headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the whitespace conventionally written after the semicolon, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz"` produces `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=xyz"]`. The removed `.strip()` was applied to the whole segment *before* `partition("=")`, so it normalised the key as well as the value \u2014 it was not redundant. Without it, `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 is never true for the overwhelmingly common header form, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and multipart form fields/file uploads are silently dropped with no error. Restore the strip (`field.strip().partition("=")`), or at minimum strip `k` and `v` individually after partitioning.

findings.title: Dropping strip() creates a multipart boundary parser differential
findings.body:
Entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; sink is the boundary value handed to `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6.

For the conforming header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----X`, `content_type.split(";")` yields `" boundary=----X"`. With `.strip()` removed, `k` is `" boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop falls through, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request body is silently discarded — no error is raised and the handler sees empty arguments/files. Conversely, a client that omits the space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=X`) still gets parsed, and trailing whitespace such as `boundary=X ` (previously removed by the strip on the whole field) is now passed into `_parse_mime_body` as part of the boundary token.

The security consequence is the divergence, not just the breakage: an attacker controls the exact spelling of the header, so they can choose whether Tornado parses the body or ignores it while an upstream proxy, WAF or upload scanner — which follows RFC 2045 and strips optional whitespace around parameters — parses it the other way. Any control implemented in front of the app that inspects multipart parts, or any application check that reasons about the presence of uploaded fields, can be steered by the choice of one space character.

Restore the whitespace handling, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` and compare `k.strip().lower() == "boundary"`, keeping `v` stripped (and quote-stripped) before it reaches `_parse_mime_body`.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace after semicolon
findings.body: The diff removes .strip() before partitioning the Content-Type field on '='. Multipart headers commonly look like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' with a space after the semicolon, so k would become ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', breaking the k == "boundary" check. No test in this PR (or apparently in the repo, since none is included) exercises this code path with a space-separated parameter to catch this regression.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message with no argument
findings.body:
The interpolation argument `% url` was dropped but the `%s` placeholder remains in the string literal, so callers now see the literal text `Failed to parse: %s`. The offending URL is lost from the exception message, making parse failures undiagnosable from logs, and the dangling placeholder looks like a formatting bug to anyone reading it. If the intent was to shorten the message, remove the placeholder too (e.g. `raise LocationParseError(url)` or `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should be retained, restore `% url`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dangling %s placeholder left in LocationParseError message

findings.title: No test covers the invalid-port parse-error path
findings.body: The diff changes `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`, dropping the `% url` substitution. This will raise a `TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting` at runtime instead of the intended `LocationParseError`, whenever a URL with a non-digit port reaches this branch. No test file is included in this PR, so nothing in the suite exercises the 'port is not a digit' branch to catch this regression before it reaches production.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string into shell=True mis-parses or executes arbitrary input
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by interpolating `name` and `directory` into a string that is then run with `shell=True`. For any reachable input containing whitespace the shell re-splits the arguments: `create_archive("my backup", "/data")` runs `tar -czf /exports/my backup.tar.gz /data`, which archives `/data` and `backup.tar.gz` into a file called `/exports/my` — silently wrong output, not an error. Input containing `;`, `|`, `$(...)` or a leading `-` is worse: `create_archive("a; rm -rf /exports", ...)` executes the second command, and `check=True` will still report success for the tar portion.

Use the argv form as `list_exports` on line 5 already does: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory], check=True)`, and reject or sanitise `name` values containing path separators so they cannot escape `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shell command built by f-string interpolation in create_archive

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and runs it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change to the command construction (or a fix for the injection risk) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: CORS allowlist widened to `*` while credentials are enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, abandoning the `ALLOWED` allowlist that the existing export on lines 6–7 enforces. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin reads from every origin on the internet, and because credentials are enabled the intent is clearly that cookies/`Authorization` ride along — so any page a logged-in user visits can drive authenticated requests against those routes and read the responses, defeating same-origin protection and any cookie-based CSRF assumption.

Note that the two options are also mutually contradictory: the CORS spec forbids `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests, so depending on how the underlying `cors` implementation resolves this the result is either (a) the dashboard is silently broken for credentialed calls, or (b) the middleware reflects the request `Origin` header, which is the fully exploitable case. Both outcomes are bad.

Fix: add the dashboard origin to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing configured middleware, or give `dashboardCors` an explicit allowlist / origin-callback that validates against a fixed set of hostnames. Never combine a wildcard or reflected origin with `credentials: true`.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent making a request with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`) treats a wildcard ACAO as a failure and blocks the response, so the very use case in the PR description — the dashboard calling the API with cookies — will fail at runtime in every browser.

Replace the wildcard with the concrete dashboard origin (or a function/array that reflects the request origin only when it is in an allow-list, mirroring the `ALLOWED` value already used on line 6). Doing so both makes credentialed requests actually work and avoids exposing the credentialed API surface to arbitrary origins.

findings.title: No test guards the new wildcard+credentials CORS config
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that is invalid per the Fetch/CORS spec (browsers will reject it) and is a common source of security regressions when 'fixed' incorrectly later. There is no test in this diff verifying the actual response headers produced by this middleware (e.g., that `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` reflects a specific origin rather than `*`, or that credentialed requests behave as intended). If someone changes this configuration in the future — correctly or incorrectly — nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, and it replaces the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is removed in the same hunk). Anyone with read access to the repo — including CI logs, forks, and anyone who ever clones it — can issue charges and read payment data with this key.

Revert to reading the key from the environment or a secrets manager, and treat the committed value as compromised: rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard now. Note that removing it in a follow-up commit does not help — it remains in git history, so rotation is mandatory.

findings.title: Removing env lookup pins every environment to the live key
findings.body:
`client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own key and a missing key failed loudly at call time. After this change the key is a compile-time constant named `acme_live_...`, so there is no longer any way for a non-production environment to point at a test account — CI runs and local development will authenticate against the live payment account and can issue real charges. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with the constant only as a documented test default), so the key remains per-environment and an unconfigured environment fails instead of silently going live.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function behavior changed without documentation

findings.title: No test verifies client() reads key from environment/config
findings.body: The change to client() replaces reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY from the environment with a hardcoded literal. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts acmepay.api_key is set from an external/configurable source rather than a fixed constant, so this regression would pass silently. The only new file, tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, is a fixture returning a dict and contains no assertions — it cannot fail.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module itself (callers therefore do `client().charge(...)` or similar attribute access), but `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`. Any test that substitutes `fake_client` for `client` will fail with `AttributeError`/`TypeError` rather than exercising the code under test, and the fixture also does nothing to prevent the real module's `api_key` from being set. Make the fixture return an object that mirrors the module's interface (e.g. a stub/`SimpleNamespace` with the methods callers use).

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified JWT, allowing tenant spoofing
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, which skips signature checking entirely (and with it exp/nbf validation). Any caller that uses the returned `tenant_id` to scope data access or authorisation is acting on a value the client can forge: crafting a token with an arbitrary `tenant_id` and an unchecked signature is trivial. The verified path already exists one function up — derive the tenant from it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation is avoiding the `public_key()` round-trip, cache the key rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: Public function reads unverified JWT claims without documenting the security risk
findings.body: The `tenant_of()` function is publicly exported but has no docstring explaining that it decodes the JWT without signature verification. A caller might reasonably assume this function returns a trustworthy tenant_id (especially given the parallel `claims_for()` function which does verify), when in fact it reads and returns data that could have been tampered with. The unverified claim should be documented explicitly, or the function should be marked private with a leading underscore.

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new behavior—reading tenant_id from an unverified JWT—but no test file is present in the diff. Nothing would catch a regression (e.g. wrong claim key, exception on malformed token, or accidental re-enabling of signature verification changing behavior). Add a test that decodes a crafted token and asserts tenant_of returns the expected tenant_id, plus a case for a missing/malformed claim.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError instead of an auth error
findings.body: Because verification is disabled, no claim-presence checks run either, so a token without a `tenant_id` claim makes line 12 raise a bare `KeyError` rather than the `jwt` exception types callers of `claims_for` would already be handling. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's auth error, so callers get a consistent failure mode.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates any user's record without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (an attacker-controlled path/query parameter) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` — with no authorisation step. `current_user(request)` is called on line 11 and the result is bound to `user` but never used; authentication is not authorisation, and `api/auth.py` documents that `require_owner` must be called on *every* object mutation. The read handler immediately above (line 6) does exactly that, so the omission here is a regression against the established pattern in the same file.

Any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's stored payment method. Fix by inserting `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `get` on line 12, before any field assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

findings.title: Public API contract violation: missing authorization check documentation
findings.body: The new `update_payment_method` function mutates a PaymentMethod object without calling `require_owner()`. The repository context establishes the contract that 'every object mutation must call this,' implying that this is a documented requirement for all public APIs that modify objects. The absence of authorization in this function contradicts the stated contract, making the function's contract with callers incomplete and misleading about what authorization it provides.

findings.title: No test exercises update_payment_method's ownership enforcement
findings.body: update_payment_method never calls require_owner (unlike the neighboring get_payment_method at line 6), so any signed-in user could update another user's payment method. No test in this diff exercises this function at all, meaning a cross-user update would silently pass. Add a test that asserts a non-owner request is rejected (e.g., raises Forbidden) and that an owner's update succeeds.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
Removing @rate_limit leaves send_reset_email unbounded per requester
findings.body: The decorator was the only thing bounding invocations of `send_reset_email` for a given caller/email. An email-provider quota is enforced per sending account and per unit time across all recipients, not per requesting client or per target address, so it does not reproduce the "5/hour per requester" behaviour the decorator provided. Two concrete consequences: (1) a single target address can be driven to arbitrarily many reset emails, and if `send_reset_email` mints a fresh token each call, every call invalidates the previous one, so a user following an earlier link gets a dead token; (2) once the provider quota is hit the failure surfaces inside `send_reset_email`, where nothing in this function handles it — `request_reset` either raises or still returns `{"sent": True}` depending on that callee, so provider throttling degrades into an unreported failure rather than a clean rejection. If the limiter is genuinely redundant, that should be demonstrated by showing where the per-requester bound now lives; otherwise keep the decorator or move an equivalent bound into `send_reset_email`.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing missing rate limiting
findings.body: The rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test changes. There is no visible test asserting that repeated calls to request_reset are throttled (or intentionally not throttled), so a future regression—either reintroducing unwanted limiting or silently reverting this removal—would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing traversal outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export` (line 14) resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` joins `name` onto `EXPORT_ROOT` directly. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Since the PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", this is evidently meant to behave the same way — route it through `_confined(name)` as well:

    path = _confined(name)
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        return fh.read(limit)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path bypasses _confined, allowing path traversal reads

findings.title: New preview path lacks any test and skips path confinement used elsewhere
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) instead of calling _confined(name) like the existing read function above. No test exercises this function, so a regression (or the missing confinement itself) would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export leaks other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` from the caller, loads each `Report` by id, and now serialises all of them with no tenant check. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `obj.tenant_id != user.tenant_id -> Forbidden` was deleted, and the import on line 1 dropped with it. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report ids and read another tenant's data through `r.to_dict()`.

Authentication is not authorisation: `current_user(request)` only establishes who is calling, not what they may read. Restore the check before serialising, e.g. keep the loop, or push the tenant filter into the load (`Report.get_for_tenant(rid, user.tenant_id)`) so the fast path is still one query without dropping the control. If the motivation was performance, a single batched query filtered by `tenant_id` gives the speedup and preserves the invariant.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer filters reports by tenant ownership

findings.title: Public API contract: bulk_export authorization removed without documenting it
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public API endpoint (called via HTTP in a request handler). Its authorization contract has changed: it previously enforced that the caller could only export reports they own (via `require_owner` on each report), and now does not. There is no docstring on this function documenting what authorization checks apply, and the removal of the check is not documented in comments or a docstring explaining why this is safe. A caller or maintainer reading this function cannot determine from its signature, name, or any documentation what data access is actually allowed.

findings.title: No test guards against cross-tenant export after authz removal
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report `require_owner` check from `bulk_export`, so a user can now request report_ids belonging to another tenant and get them back. No test in this change (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is shown) asserts that `bulk_export` rejects or filters out reports not owned by the caller. If this change is wrong, nothing would fail: there is no test that calls `bulk_export` with a foreign-tenant report_id and checks for a Forbidden error or filtered result.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing/db.py.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows it by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string on line 9 and calls `execute(sql)` with no params on line 10.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is broken for plainly legitimate input: a customer named `O'Brien` terminates the single-quoted literal and the statement fails with a syntax error, and a `status` of `None` interpolates the literal text `'None'` rather than a NULL comparison. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` so the driver binds both values.

findings.title: SQL injection in search_customers via f-string interpolation
Public API contract undocumented for search_customers
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a public entry point but lacks documentation of its parameters (`term`, `status`) and return value. A caller cannot reliably determine what the function does or what data structure it returns without reading the implementation. Additionally, the function violates the established module pattern: the docstring on `execute()` (line 2 of db.py) states "params must carry every caller value," but this function passes raw `term` and `status` values directly into an f-string instead of as parameterized arguments, making the contract unclear and the safety properties violated.

findings.title: No test coverage for new search_customers function
findings.body: search_customers is new, unparameterized SQL-building logic with no accompanying test. Nothing verifies its query construction, its handling of special characters in `term`/`status` (e.g. quotes, %, or SQL metacharacters), or that it returns expected results. Since it deviates from the parameterized pattern used in get_customer, a test asserting on the generated SQL/params would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The existing delivery function on lines 8-10 refuses to issue a request unless `host` is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of tenant-supplied URL and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no parsing and no allowlist check, so a registered target of `http://169.254.169.254/...` or an internal host is fetched by the server. Since the PR description says tenants register this URL themselves, the input is attacker-controlled. Extract the parse-and-check logic from the send path into a helper and call it from both functions before any request is made. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a redirect from an allowed host would defeat a check applied only to the initial URL.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check — SSRF

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that issues an outbound GET to an arbitrary URL, unlike the existing post() which validates host against ALLOWED_HOSTS first (lines 8-9). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing to catch a future regression, a change in behavior, or the fact that this function currently performs no allowlist check before making the request.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable URLs
findings.body: The return type promises an HTTP status code, but for the cases this function most needs to handle — DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, or the 5s timeout firing — `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`/`Timeout` and no status code is ever produced. A caller written as `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200:` will propagate an exception out of a validation step rather than reporting the endpoint as unverified. Wrap the call in `try/except requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or `None`) that callers can distinguish, or document that the function raises and fix the callers accordingly. Note also that a malformed or non-HTTP scheme in the tenant-supplied URL raises `MissingSchema`/`InvalidURL` from the same line.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, and `restrict_public_buckets`. This is the account-level safety net that prevents a public ACL or a wildcard-principal bucket policy from ever taking effect. With it off, any later `aws-cli put-object-acl --acl public-read`, any misconfigured upload path, or any bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` will silently succeed and expose customer invoices — documents that typically contain names, addresses, amounts and account identifiers — to anonymous readers on the internet.

This bucket is also unrelated to the PR's stated purpose ("public assets bucket for the marketing site"); nothing in the description justifies a customer-invoices bucket, let alone a publicly-reachable one.

Recommended: either drop the `invoices` resources from this PR entirely, or set all four flags to `true` (the secure default) for the invoices bucket and restrict access via IAM/pre-signed URLs. Keep the `false` settings scoped strictly to the marketing assets bucket if they are genuinely required there.

I cannot see any bucket policy or ACL in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the objects are public *today*; the finding is that the control preventing them from becoming public has been switched off on a bucket holding sensitive data.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Customer invoices bucket added with all public-access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 digest as `verify_stripe` (line 11 is identical to line 6) but validates it with `expected == header` rather than `hmac.compare_digest`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, permitting byte-by-byte forgery of a valid webhook signature without knowing the secret. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the sibling function. Note that `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None` or non-str/bytes `header`, so if callers can pass a missing header, guard for that at the same time.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ HMAC compared with `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest

findings.title: Public function signature implies same security properties as sibling
findings.body: The `verify_acmepay` function appears to provide the same service as `verify_stripe` (webhook signature verification), but uses timing-unsafe string comparison (`==`) instead of the constant-time `hmac.compare_digest()` used by `verify_stripe`. A caller who treats these functions interchangeably — a reasonable assumption given identical names and signatures — will inadvertently introduce a timing attack vulnerability. The function's name and parameters do not communicate this critical difference in security properties.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no accompanying tests
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new behavior (mirroring verify_stripe but using == instead of hmac.compare_digest) and no test file is included in this diff. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. inverted, wrong hash, or accepting mismatched signatures), nothing in this change would fail. Since verify_stripe presumably has tests elsewhere validating correct/incorrect signature handling, the same coverage should be added for verify_acmepay.

findings.title: Full traceback and exception text returned to HTTP clients
findings.body:
`handle()` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response body. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception receives the source file paths, module layout, line numbers, framework/library versions implied by the frames, and whatever the exception message contains — which for database, HTTP-client or credential-handling errors routinely includes SQL fragments, internal hostnames, connection strings or partial tokens. That is a free reconnaissance primitive for an attacker probing the API, and it turns any input-validation bug into a mapping exercise for the codebase.

The stated goal (on-call visibility without SSH) is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which puts the same traceback in the log pipeline. Keep the client-facing body generic and correlate via an identifier instead, e.g. generate a request/error id, log it alongside the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "error_id": <id>}, 500`. If detailed bodies are genuinely wanted in development, gate them behind an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than emitting them unconditionally.
