findings.title: No test covers the new response body containing exception/traceback
findings.body: The `handle` function now returns exception details and a full traceback in the response body instead of a generic message. This is a security-relevant behavior change (information disclosure) that has no accompanying test verifying the response shape, content, or that it's gated appropriately. Without a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce or remove this behavior with nothing failing either way.

findings.title: hash_reset_password emits MD5, incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If a reset flow stores the result of `hash_reset_password` in the same column that login later checks with `bcrypt.checkpw`, verification cannot succeed \u2014 `bcrypt.checkpw` raises `ValueError: invalid salt` on a non-bcrypt hash rather than returning `False`, so the login path errors instead of rejecting. Conversely, if a separate verifier re-hashes with MD5, the password is stored unsalted with a hash that is trivially brute-forced/rainbow-tabled, which is unacceptable for a credential even in a reset context. Use the same `bcrypt.hashpw`/`gensalt` path as `hash_password` (or drop the function and call `hash_password`); if the intent was a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, name and implement it as a token digest with `secrets.token_urlsafe` + SHA-256, not MD5 of a user password.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` stores/derives a password digest with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast general-purpose hash — commodity GPUs compute billions of candidates per second — and with no salt the output is also vulnerable to rainbow-table and cross-account correlation attacks (identical passwords produce identical digests). Anyone who obtains the stored value, via a database dump, backup, or log, recovers the plaintext for most real-world passwords in minutes.

The same module already does this correctly on line 7: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. There is no reason for the reset path to differ. Delete `hash_reset_password` and call `hash_password` from the reset flow; if the reset flow actually needs a one-time token rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe()` and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`, not with a hash of user-supplied input.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm whether the digest is persisted or compared — but either use of MD5 over a password is wrong.

(The `checksum` helper on lines 14-16 uses SHA-256 over file contents, which is an appropriate non-password use.)

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new, security-relevant code path (used presumably to verify reset tokens/passwords) with zero tests. Nothing would fail if this function were changed to return a constant, throw, or use a different algorithm entirely. At minimum a test should assert that hashing is deterministic/non-deterministic as intended and that it can be verified correctly.

findings.title: Public password utility lacks documented contract
findings.body: The `hash_reset_password` function is a public API next to `hash_password`, but has no docstring explaining its contract, parameters, or return value. A caller needs to know whether this function is safe to use and for what purpose (e.g., is this for actual password storage, or just reset tokens?).

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with NPM_TOKEN and write token
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets` and, unlike `pull_request`, the `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read/write even for pull requests from forks. Lines 11-12 then deliberately check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker-controlled commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14-15.

Any external contributor can open a PR that rewrites `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources, including `package.json` lifecycle scripts or lockfile-resolved dependencies) and exfiltrate `NPM_TOKEN`. Because `actions/checkout` persists credentials by default, the write-capable `GITHUB_TOKEN` is also left in `.git/config` inside the untrusted working tree and can be used to push to the repository.

To give forks the same signal safely, either:
- revert to `pull_request` (fork runs get a read-only token and no secrets — the size check does not obviously need `NPM_TOKEN`, and if it needs a registry credential, move the privileged part to a separate `workflow_run` job that consumes an artifact), or
- keep `pull_request_target` but do **not** check out the head SHA and do **not** run any script from it; only use it for operations on trusted base-branch code.

If the head checkout must stay, at minimum add `permissions: contents: read`, `persist-credentials: false` on the checkout, and remove the `NPM_TOKEN` from the step that executes untrusted code.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with repo secrets

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values; hashable-but-unserialisable now raises
findings.body: The old key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any hashable value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, frozensets, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. The new key runs `json.dumps` over the whole context, so any such value now raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from inside `cached_render`, before rendering is even attempted. A caller that previously rendered fine now gets an exception from the cache layer. If contexts really can contain arbitrary objects, pass `default=repr` (or a `cls=` encoder) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key makes collisions serve the wrong render
findings.body:
`cached_render` now collapses `(template_source, context)` into an MD5 hexdigest instead of comparing the values exactly. With the tuple key, two distinct inputs could never alias; with a digest key, any collision causes the second caller to receive the first caller's rendered output. MD5 chosen-prefix collisions are cheap in practice, so if `template_source` or the context values can be influenced by an untrusted party (user-authored templates, multi-tenant snippets), a crafted pair of inputs can read back a render produced for someone else's input.

The fix costs nothing: use `hashlib.sha256(...)` or `hashlib.blake2b(payload.encode(), digest_size=16)`. If you keep MD5 for speed, pass `usedforsecurity=False` so the call does not fail on FIPS-enabled interpreters — that flag also documents the intent for the next reader.

I cannot see any caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the inputs are attacker-reachable; if `template_source` is always a trusted, in-repo constant this is a hardening nit rather than a defect.

findings.title: No test for contexts with non-JSON-serializable values
findings.body: The old key `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` only required dict values to be comparable when keys tie (rare), so arbitrary objects worked. The new key building via `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)` requires every value in `context` to be JSON-serializable, or `cached_render` now raises `TypeError` where it previously succeeded. None of the added tests exercise a context with a non-serializable value, so this behavior change would go unnoticed until it breaks a caller in production.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded by the shell
findings.body: The old form interpolated `directory` into a shell string, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"`, `"/srv/data/*"`, or anything containing `$HOME`/`~` got shell word-splitting, globbing and expansion for free. In the list form `directory` is passed to tar as a single literal path operand, and `--` further guarantees no interpretation. Any such caller now gets `tar: /srv/a /srv/b: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, with `check=True`, a `CalledProcessError` instead of a working archive. If multi-path or glob inputs are in use, change the signature to accept a sequence of paths (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`) and update callers; if not, it is worth asserting that in the docstring.

findings.title: `directory` operand is unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, but `directory` is passed straight through to tar as a path operand with no check. Because it is an argv element after `--`, there is no command or option injection here 	so this is not a re-introduction of the original bug. The residual risk is scope: if `directory` is caller-supplied, a request can cause tar to read any path the service can read (e.g. `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, `/proc/self/environ`) and write it into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is presumably a served or retrievable location. If `directory` is only ever an internal constant, this is a non-issue.

Suggest either documenting that `directory` must be trusted, or resolving it with `os.path.realpath` and asserting it stays under an expected export root before invoking tar.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New name allowlist rejects previously-valid names and raises TypeError on non-str

findings.title: No test verifies the constructed argv list, only the shell flag
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` only asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs['shell'] is False`; it never inspects the positional command list. Nothing checks that the list actually contains `['tar', '-czf', '/exports/nightly.tar.gz', '--', '/srv/data']`, and in particular nothing exercises the `--` separator that is the actual defense against a `directory` value like `-C/etc` being parsed as a tar flag. If a future edit dropped the `--` or mis-ordered the args (still calling subprocess.run with shell=False), this test suite would keep passing.

findings.title: `spy` fixture is not defined by this change
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` takes a `spy` fixture that is neither a pytest builtin nor added by this PR (only two files changed, no `conftest.py`). If it does not already exist the test errors at collection; if it does exist but does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test shells out to real `tar` against `/exports` and will fail in CI. Either add the fixture or use `monkeypatch`/`unittest.mock.patch` on `subprocess.run` directly. While there, assert the first argument is a list starting with `"tar"` — `shell is False` alone does not pin the argv shape that makes this change safe.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. It passes for any return value, so it only detects a raised exception; it would pass equally if `render` returned `None`, an empty string, or a malformed document for the blank-invoice case. Given the PR description says this covers "the blank-invoice case", assert the expected output explicitly (e.g. `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == ""` or whatever the documented empty rendering is), so a regression in the empty path is actually caught.

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing tie-rounding test deleted instead of updated to new behaviour
findings.body:
The only assertion covering the exact half-way case (`Decimal("2.345")`, a tie between 2.34 and 2.35) has been removed, and this diff contains no change to `round_cents` itself. Two possibilities, both problems: either the rounding fix is not in this PR and the test was deleted purely to make CI green, or the fix landed elsewhere and the correct action was to update the expected value (e.g. to `Decimal("2.35")` for half-up) rather than delete the case. findings.title: Retry test patches the wrong target, so the real deliver() runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds the function object into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` still calls the original object it captured. This test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times (possible real network/side-effectful sends in CI) and asserts `False` only because the real call happens to fail — it would silently stop testing the retry-exhaustion path the moment the real transport succeeds or raises.

Use the same target as the passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times, so the test actually pins the retry count rather than just the return value.

findings.body: The test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly states that patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect the module because `deliver` is bound into `notify.sender`'s namespace at import time. The first test correctly patches `notify.sender.deliver`. This test will not exercise the retry path as intended—it will pass even if retries are broken. Change the patch target to `notify.sender.deliver` to match the documented behavior and the pattern in the passing test.

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper added immediately below it. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote — a free-text field, a formatted number like `1,234`, a quoted string — will split into extra columns or unbalance quoting, silently corrupting the output for downstream parsers. The fix is to route each cell through `csv_escape`, i.e. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

Note also that `csv_escape` assumes a string: `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for an int or `None`, so the coercion must stay on the caller side (or move inside `csv_escape`) when they are wired together.

findings.title: csv_rows joins field values without applying csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, never calling the `csv_escape` helper defined a few lines below. Any field value that itself contains a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns or corrupt quoting in the emitted record, letting whoever controls a row value inject additional columns into the output consumed downstream (spreadsheet, ETL loader, diff tooling). Wrap each field: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. While you are there, consider also neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to avoid formula injection when the file is opened in a spreadsheet, and note that `csv_escape` currently assumes a `str` argument (it will raise on non-string input unless coerced first, which the suggested fix does). The row data source is not visible in this diff or the retrieved context, so the degree of attacker control is unconfirmed.

findings.title: dump_streaming yields nothing for empty rows; chunk_size=0 raises
findings.body:
For `rows == []`, `range(0, 0, chunk_size)` is empty, so the generator terminates without yielding anything. A caller that writes the stream to a file or a response body ends up with zero bytes rather than `"[]"`, which is not parseable JSON — the non-streaming `dump([])` returns `"[]"`, so the two entry points disagree on the empty case. Consider yielding `json.dumps([])` when `rows` is empty.

Separately, `chunk_size=0` (or negative) makes `range` raise `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` rather than a meaningful error; a guard on the parameter would be cheap.

findings.title: New exporter logic added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width all contain real logic (column ordering, quoting rules, chunking, margin arithmetic) but none are covered by any test in this diff. The repo does have a test for csv_header, showing exporter functions are expected to be tested; a bug in any of these (e.g. off-by-one in chunking, wrong quote escaping, incorrect margin math) would currently pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Test cannot meaningfully fail: no controlled 'now', trivial assertion
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which passes an explicit `now=` to freeze the expiry check at a specific point, this new test calls `is_expired(token.expires_at)` with no `now` argument and checks it immediately after issuing a token. Since the token was just issued, it will always be far from expiry regardless of whether the expiry-window logic is correct — the assertion cannot catch a real boundary bug (e.g. an off-by-one in the expiry window). The `token.issued_at.date() == datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` check is similarly not exercising the 'still valid inside the expiry window' behaviour the PR claims to test; it only checks issuance timestamp, and is itself vulnerable to flaking around UTC midnight since two separate `datetime.now()` calls are compared.

findings.title: `is_expired` called without `now=` and with a different argument than the sibling test

Line 12 passes `token.expires_at` with no `now`, so it depends on (a) `now` having a default that reads the real clock and (b) the first positional parameter meaning "expiry instant" rather than "issued instant". If either assumption is wrong the test raises `TypeError` or asserts the opposite of what it reads. Please confirm the signature and pass `now=` explicitly for consistency with line 6.

findings.title: Expiry check breaks on missing, null or naive expires_at
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` imposes three new requirements on every coupon object reaching `apply_coupon`: the attribute must exist, it must not be `None`, and it must be timezone-aware. Any coupon lacking the attribute raises `AttributeError`; `None` or a naive datetime raises `TypeError` ("can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes") — both surface as a 500-style crash rather than the intended `CouponExpired`. The fact that the existing test had to be amended to pass `expires_at=tomorrow()` is direct evidence that coupons were previously constructed without it, so other construction sites and persisted rows may also lack it. Guard the branch, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.
